lines.trans: No, hold on! Are these my husband's organs here?
Did my husband use everything that is inside here?
Did he really use them? Sometimes inside us comes a lot of spare parts.

words.gram: contraction of a + as in às vezes

lines.trans: You know those shirts we wear that have a button at the bottom?

words.gram: feminine singular article in a gente

lines.trans: If a button falls off, you take the button from the bottom.
Doctor, just a second, I am going to interrupt you.
My husband is a man, he is human!
I am human too, honey. I am a doctor! But everything is going to be fine with him.
Okay, but what do I do with this here now?
You keep it in the freezer, separate from the meat, so as not to mix them up.
No, hold on! Are these my husband's organs here?
Did my husband use everything that is inside here?
Did he really use them? Sometimes inside us comes a lot of spare parts.

Doctor, just a second, I am going to interrupt you.
My husband is a man, he is human!
I am human too, honey. I am a doctor! But everything is going to be fine with him.
Okay, but what do I do with this here now?
You keep it in the freezer, separate from the meat, so as not to mix them up.
Bye!

meanings.note: Links verbs like faltar to an event or destination.

examples.trans: She missed a meeting.
In an hour.

meanings.note: Marks the current moment resulting from an earlier action.

examples.trans: Now she is in a meeting.

examples.text: Agora tenho que resolver umas coisinhas.
examples.trans: Right now I have to sort out a few little things.

meanings.note: Used both for love and as an affectionate vocative ('honey, darling').

examples.trans: I am human too, honey.
My love, what is this?

meanings.note: Points to the speaker's location or reinforces demonstratives like isso aqui and esse slide aqui.

examples.text: Ela veio aqui olhar um extintor.
examples.trans: She came here to check an extinguisher.
This here is a chart.

meanings.note: Used in de baixo ('from the bottom; lower').

examples.text: Você tira o botão de baixo.
examples.trans: You take the bottom button.

examples.text: Ele mora no andar de baixo.
examples.trans: He lives on the floor below.

meanings.note: Modifies a verb to mean well or carefully, as in olhar bem (look closely).

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.
Everything is fine around here.

meanings.note: Plural botões; covers clothing buttons and push buttons.

examples.text: Se cair um botão, você tira outro.
examples.trans: If a button falls off, you take another.

examples.text: A camisa tem um botão embaixo.
examples.trans: The shirt has a button at the bottom.

meanings.note: Used for objects dropping or buttons coming loose.

examples.text: Se cair um botão, você tira outro.
examples.trans: If a button falls off, you take another.
The phone fell on the floor.

meanings.note: Button-down or dress shirt.

examples.text: Essas camisas que a gente usa têm botão.
examples.trans: These shirts that we wear have a button.
He bought a new shirt.

meanings.note: Everyday culinary word for meat, especially beef.

examples.trans: Store it separately from the meat.
I am not eating meat today.

meanings.note: Marks accompaniment or an added ingredient such as sweetener.

examples.trans: I want coffee with sweetener.

examples.text: Ela está com a nossa equipe.
examples.trans: She is with our team.

meanings.note: Often used with com when mistaking one thing for another.

examples.trans: Store it separately so as not to mix it up.
That confuses everyone.

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.

examples.trans: It’s a marketing meeting.
I’m in finance.

meanings.note: Indicates the interior of a room or space, often paired with lá or para.

examples.trans: Look inside there.
Everyone is inside there.

meanings.note: Respectful title for physicians and often used politely for men.

examples.text: Ai, doutor! Como foi a cirurgia?
examples.trans: Oh, doctor! How was the surgery?
Doctor, these here are organs!

meanings.note: Third-person masculine singular subject pronoun.

examples.trans: He isn't coming anymore.
He canceled the meeting.

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.

examples.trans: He is in the meeting.
She stays on her phone.

meanings.note: Written as one word when meaning 'underneath / down below'.

examples.text: As camisas têm um botão embaixo.
examples.trans: The shirts have a button at the bottom.
The box is down below.

meanings.note: Demonstrative determiner; in spoken Brazilian Portuguese esse commonly covers both this near me and that just mentioned.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

examples.text: Vou ficar sentado esse tempo inteiro.
examples.trans: I'm going to stay seated that whole time.

meanings.note: Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.

examples.trans: I’m in finance.
I’m not going.

meanings.note: Irregular past eu fiz (I made/did); não tem o que fazer means having nothing to do.

examples.text: Ela não tem o que fazer agora.
examples.trans: She has nothing to do now.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

meanings.note: Expresses staying in a place or state (ficar sentado, fica no celular).

examples.trans: You're going to stay seated.

examples.text: Ela fica no celular o dia todo.
examples.trans: She stays on her phone all day.

meanings.note: Common English loanword in Brazil for a deep freezer.

examples.trans: You keep it in the freezer.
The ice cream is in the freezer.

meanings.note: Alone as vocative gente! it means folks/guys; with article a gente it means we/us with third-person singular verbs.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?
Oh, folks, the meeting ran late.

meanings.note: Standard Brazilian verb for putting something away in storage.

examples.trans: You keep it in the freezer.
Store it separately from the meat.

meanings.note: Adult male human; plural homens.

examples.trans: My husband is a man!
That man works here.

meanings.note: Silent initial h.

examples.text: Meu marido é um homem, é humano!
examples.trans: My husband is a man, he is human!
I am human too, honey.

meanings.note: Used when cutting into someone's speech.

examples.text: Só um segundo, vou te interromper.
examples.trans: Just a second, I am going to interrupt you.
Sorry to interrupt the meeting.

meanings.note: Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.

examples.trans: I’m going to the meeting.
Aren’t you going?

meanings.note: Neutral demonstrative pronoun pointing to what was just said or done.

examples.trans: What is this, man?
That slows everyone else down.

meanings.note: A married man in relation to his spouse.

examples.text: Como é que tá meu marido?
examples.trans: How is my husband doing?
Your husband is already doing wonderfully.

meanings.note: Introduces a contrast. The informal thanks softens the refusal; it does not accept the invitation.

examples.trans: I’m not going, but thanks.
It’s a meeting, but I’m not going.

meanings.note: First-person singular possessive agreeing with the thing possessed.

examples.text: O seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?
That is my job.

meanings.note: Agrees with its noun as a determiner/adjective; singular muita coisa idiomatically means many things.

examples.trans: They say a lot of things.
I have many numbers here.

meanings.note: Medical doctor.

examples.text: Sou médico! Vai ficar tudo bem.
examples.trans: I am a doctor! Everything will be fine.

examples.text: O médico falou com a família.
examples.trans: The doctor spoke with the family.

meanings.note: A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.

examples.trans: No, I’m not going.
Aren’t you going?

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: What is your job title?
Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Spoken fusion of espera aí ('wait there / hang on').

examples.text: Não, peraí! Isso aqui são órgãos?
examples.trans: No, hold on! Are these organs here?
Hang on, I will be right back.

meanings.note: In peça de reposição, a spare or replacement part.

examples.trans: A lot of spare parts come included.
A piece is missing here.

meanings.note: Informal reduced para. Before a feminine noun, this Brazilian spelling can also represent a contraction including the article a; the exact meeting is clear from context.

examples.trans: I’m going to the meeting.
Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.
What is this, man?

meanings.note: In peça de reposição, a spare part.

examples.trans: A lot of spare parts come inside.
We need stock replacement.

meanings.note: Covers knowing facts or finding out information.

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.
Do you know the answer?

meanings.note: Introduces a condition; triggers future subjunctive when referring to a possible future action (se vocês olharem).

examples.text: Se eu vou entrar, você vai também.
examples.trans: If I'm going in, you're going too.

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: A brief moment of time.

examples.trans: Doctor, just one second!
Wait a second, please.

meanings.note: Used with de for keeping things apart.

examples.trans: Store it separately from the meat.
They live in separate houses.

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.

examples.trans: I’m in finance.
It’s a marketing meeting.

meanings.note: Limits a statement (eu só quero) or forms só que (except that / the catch is).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

examples.text: Só que agora ela precisa de ajuda.
examples.trans: Except now she needs help.

meanings.note: Adds another person or item to what was already stated.

examples.trans: I want you to go in too.
I'm the one who made it too!

meanings.note: Everyday friendly farewell across Brazil, borrowed long ago from Italian ciao.

examples.trans: Bye, see you tomorrow!
Bye, folks!

meanings.note: Informal singular object pronoun, routinely mixed with você in warm everyday Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.
examples.trans: Let me tell you something.
I'll help you later.

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.
There are some good numbers.

meanings.note: Everyday verb for removing or taking something out.

examples.trans: We took it out during surgery.

examples.text: Você tira o botão de baixo.
examples.trans: You take the button from the bottom.

meanings.note: Informal singular 'you', often paired with third-person verb forms in casual Rio speech.

examples.trans: You keep it in the freezer.

examples.text: Depois que tu estica, fica difícil.
examples.trans: Once you stretch it, it gets hard.

meanings.note: Neutral pronoun for 'everything / all of it'.

examples.trans: It was all inside him.

examples.text: Vai ficar tudo bem com ele.
examples.trans: Everything is going to be fine with him.

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?
There are some good numbers.

meanings.note: Covers both using a tool/organ and wearing clothes.

examples.text: Essas camisas que a gente usa têm botão.
examples.trans: These shirts that we wear have a button.
Did my husband use all of this?

meanings.note: In às vezes, means 'sometimes'.

examples.text: Às vezes vem muita peça extra.
examples.trans: Sometimes a lot of spare parts come.
I already said that twice.

meanings.note: Irregular verb: present ele vem (he comes), completed past ela veio (she came).

examples.text: Ela veio aqui olhar um extintor.
examples.trans: She came here to check an extinguisher.
He isn't coming anymore.

meanings.note: A person being addressed, with third-person verb agreement: você vai, vocês vão. Vai and vão are forms of ir, not forms of the pronoun. Common in Brazil; not a rule that every Brazilian region uses the same address system.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?
Are you in finance?

meanings.note: Plural órgãos (keeps stress on the first syllable).

examples.trans: Doctor, these here are organs!

examples.text: São os órgãos do meu marido?
examples.trans: Are these my husband's organs?
